title: None Beyond Ḍombī
summary: Kāṇha, who has rowed through the three worlds with ease and fallen asleep in the play of great bliss, turns to Ḍombī, the outcaste woman: the high-born keep to the edge while the kāpālika is in the middle; she has spoiled everything and toppled the moon; some speak ill of her, yet the wise do not let go of her neck, and there is no loose woman beyond her. Munidatta reads her here as the unpurified avadhūtī, who for yogis without the guru's lineage destroys the moon, conventional bodhicitta, but whom the lords of yogis who know her through the bliss of union never let go at the throat, the wheel of enjoyment (cp.18.m3, cp.18.m4, cp.18.m5).

flags.note: The Bengali heading gives only the rāga. The poet's name is supplied from the attribution kṛṣṇavajrapādānām ('of Kṛṣṇavajrapāda') that Shastri's text prints before the first line, which the edition's emendation removes from 1a; the Tibetan heading also names him (nag po spyod pa'i zhabs). I give the glossary form Kāṇha; 'Kṛṣṇavajrapāda' would follow the attribution's own wording, as 'Lūyīpāda' does in the model heading.

lines.gloss: three · worlds · by me · rowed (driven, carried) · with ease (in sport)
lines.en: I have rowed through the [three worlds]{trailokya} with ease;

flags.note: bāhia is the participle of bāh-, the songs' verb for rowing a boat, which can also mean drive, carry or convey. Alternatives: (a) 'rowed through' (chosen: the verb's usual sense in the songs, and the reading the glossary's entry for the three worlds already assumes); (b) 'driven off, cast aside' (vāhita), which would come closer to Munidatta's 'overcome' (bādhita); (c) the Tibetan 'I enter the three worlds without effort' ('bad med 'jug). There is no boat elsewhere in this song, so (a) may press the verb.

lines.gloss: I · slept (lay down) · great bliss · in play
lines.en: I have fallen asleep in the [play]{lila} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.

flags.note: mahāsuha līṛem̐ may be one phrase, 'in the play of great bliss' (chosen), or two, 'in great bliss, playfully'; Munidatta takes līṛem̐ alone as krīḍayā, 'in play', and the Tibetan has 'I revel (rol) in great bliss'. suteli is past, 'slept, lay down'; 'have fallen asleep' gives its present result, as Munidatta's 'therefore I am asleep' (ahaṃ suptaḥ) does.

lines.gloss: what kind of · hey (vocative, to a woman) · Ḍombī · your · bhābhariālī (sense uncertain)
lines.en: Hey [Ḍombī]{dombi}, what kind of [bhābhariālī]{bhabhariali} is yours?

flags.note: bhābhariālī is kept in its source form, as the glossary directs: its sense is unknown. Munidatta cites it as bharbhariālikā with 'by false imputation' (asadāropeṇa) beside it, which suggests some kind of show or pretence; the Tibetan has skra yags, apparently 'fine hair', which would make the question about her looks. Neither is certain enough to put in the line.

lines.gloss: at the edge (outside, at the end) · high-born people · in the middle · kāpālika
lines.en: At the edge, [high-born]{kulina} people; in the middle, the [kāpālika]{kapalika}.

flags.note: The line has no verb, and I keep it verbless. ante may be 'at the edge', 'outside' (Munidatta's bāhye) or 'at the end'; I chose 'at the edge' as the natural pair to mājhem̐, 'in the middle'. The Tibetan construes differently: 'the kāpāli among those born of the edge lineage' (mtha' rigs skye ba'i nang na), taking ante with kuliṇajaṇa and mājhem̐ as 'among'.

lines.gloss: you (agent) + lo (vocative particle) · Ḍombī · all · spoiled (defiled, ruined)

flags.note: biṭaliu: 'defiled' (ritual pollution by contact, the sense of later Bengali biṭāl-, which would suit an untouchable woman), or 'ruined, destroyed' (the Tibetan rnam par nyams byed; Munidatta's paraphrase has 'destroyed'). I chose 'spoiled', which can carry both. tam̐ilo is tam̐i, 'you', with the vocative lo; Munidatta's paraphrase has tayā, 'by her', but the Tibetan keeps 'you' (khyod).

lines.gloss: of deeds (works) · cause (for the sake of) · moon (hare-bearer) · toppled (shaken loose, destroyed)
lines.en: you have toppled the [moon]{moon}, the cause of deeds.

flags.note: kājaṇa kāraṇa is obscure. Chosen: kājaṇa as a genitive plural of kāja, 'deed, work', and kāraṇa 'cause', qualifying the moon, because both witnesses read a cause attached to the moon: the Tibetan 'the hare-holder that does the deed' (bya ba byed pa ri bong 'dzin pa), Munidatta 'the moon ... which has become the cause of clear light'. Alternatives: 'for the sake of deeds (or business) you toppled the moon' (kāraṇa as a postposition); or kāja ṇa kāraṇa, 'without deed or cause', i.e. 'for nothing'. ṭāliu, 'shaken from its place, toppled'; Munidatta and the Tibetan both have 'destroyed'.

lines.gloss: someone · or other · to (of) you · bad (ill) · says
lines.en: Some people speak ill of you;

flags.note: kehe keho, 'someone or other', takes a singular verb (bolai); 'some people' gives the indefinite sense. biruā is the adjective 'bad, ill' (Sanskrit virūpa), not the poet's name.

lines.translit: bidujaṇa loa torem̐ kaṇṭha na melaī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: wise · people · your · neck · not · lets go
lines.en: [the wise]{vidujana} do not let go of your [neck]{kantha}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line reads 'people of good family (rigs ldan skye bo) embrace you by the neck': a different subject, as if reading a word like kulīna for bidujaṇa, and a positive 'embrace' for 'do not let go'. The sense 'hold her in an embrace' is the same; I translate the Bengali negative as it stands. 'the wise' covers bidujaṇa loa, 'wise people'.

lines.gloss: by Kāṇha · sung · Caṇḍālī of desire

flags.note: kāhne gāitu, 'by Kāṇha sung': taken as past with present result (the Tibetan has blangs, 'sang'; Munidatta's paraphrase is present, gīyate, 'is sung'). kāmacaṇḍālī is taken as what is sung, the woman the song celebrates, as both witnesses take it ('sung the Caṇḍālī' in the sense of 'sing arms and the man'); it could also be a vocative, 'O Caṇḍālī of desire', with 5b as the words sung.

lines.gloss: Ḍombī · beyond (surpassing, apart from) · there is not · loose woman

flags.note: taāgali: 'surpassing, more than' (the Tibetan lhag pa: no low-caste woman surpasses her) or 'apart from' (Munidatta's ḍombīvyatirekāt: there is no other such woman but Ḍombī). 'Beyond' keeps both.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. The name recalls Gauḍa, an old name for part of Bengal. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song glu dbyangs chen po zhes bya ba, 'the melody called Great', and names the poet nag po spyod pa'i zhabs, its usual name for Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya).

The poet's name is not in the Bengali heading. It comes from the attribution kṛṣṇavajrapādānām, 'of Kṛṣṇavajrapāda', which Shastri's text prints at the head of the first line and which the edition's emendation removes from 1a as not part of the verse.

Munidatta introduces the song as Kṛṣṇācārya setting out 'that same meaning' again, for the sake of the ultimate, in the understanding of conventional truth, 'through the twilight language of Ḍombī' (ḍombīsandhyayā). The Tibetan translation of the comment has 'through understanding the meaning of the ultimate and the conventional truths'.

The song's words are those of caste and sexual reputation. [Ḍombī]{dombi} is a woman of the Ḍom caste, whom caste society treated as untouchable; the [high-born]{kulina} are people of good family, bound by purity rules; the [kāpālika]{kapalika} is an ascetic who ignores those rules; a [Caṇḍālī]{candali} is a woman of the community ranked lowest of all; and chiṇālī is a term of abuse for an unchaste woman. The speaker's address mixes reproach (couplet 3) with praise (couplets 4 and 5).

bāhia is the past participle of bāh-, the verb the songs use for rowing a boat; it can also mean drive, carry or convey. With mai, 'by me', it gives 'I have rowed'. helem̐ (Sanskrit helā, 'sport, ease, carelessness') is 'with ease' or 'in sport'. Since no boat appears elsewhere in this song, 'passed through' or 'driven off' (as if from vāhita) remain possible.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line sa gsum po la bdag ni 'bad med 'jug, 'I enter the three worlds without effort', taking bāhia as 'enter' and helem̐ as 'without effort'. Munidatta's gloss has neither rowing nor entering: the fault belonging to the three worlds 'has been overcome with ease' (avahelayā bādhitaḥ), as though he heard bāhia as a form of bādh-, 'repel, suppress' (cp.18.m2).

Munidatta reads the [three worlds]{trailokya} as [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}: through attachment to the [vajra woman]{vajravanita}, Kṛṣṇācārya has overcome with ease their fault of the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti}, 'and therefore I am asleep'. He glosses līṛem̐ as krīḍayā, 'in play', and takes the sleep as [yogic sleep]{yoganidra}, entered through understanding the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya} (nairātmadharma) (cp.18.m2).

The Tibetan line has bdag ni nyal nas bde ba chen pos rol, 'having lain down, I revel in great bliss'. The Tibetan of Munidatta's comment renders yoganidrā as 'the yogin went to sleep' (rnal 'byor pa gnyid du song ba), apparently dividing the word as yogī + nidrā, and has 'the dharma of Nairātmā' (bdag med ma'i chos), the goddess, where the Sanskrit has the nature of selflessness (cp.18.m2). Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after 1b as well as after the refrain; it is not translated.

bhābhariālī: a word of uncertain sense, kept in its source form; kaisaṇi, 'of what kind', agrees with it as a feminine. Munidatta cites it as bharbhariālikā and sets 'by false imputation' (asadāropeṇa) beside it, so that the question becomes 'O Ḍombī, what have you done by false imputation?'; he gives no equation (cp.18.m3). The Tibetan translation has skra yags, apparently 'fine hair', in the line, and in the comment 'skra yags: by imputing impermanence' (mi rtag par sgro 'dogs pas).

kāpālika (the song's kābālī): an ascetic who carries a skull-bowl, wears bone ornaments, keeps to cremation grounds and disregards caste purity; Kāṇha elsewhere calls himself one. The Tibetan keeps the word (ka pA li). kuliṇajaṇa is kulīna jana, 'people of good family'. The refrain sets two places side by side without a verb: respectable people at the edge, the kāpālika at the centre.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads mtha' rigs skye ba'i nang na ka pA li, apparently 'the kāpāli among those born of the edge lineage': it takes ante with kuliṇajaṇa (mtha' 'edge', rigs 'family', skye ba 'born') and mājhem̐ as 'among'. That would place the kāpālika among people of the border castes rather than set him over against the high-born. The division of the Tibetan phrase is not certain.

Munidatta says that with the refrain Kāṇha turns to the unpurified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (the central channel of the subtle body, here in its unpurified state). He divides kuliṇa into ku, 'in ku, the body' (kau śarīre), and līna, 'absorbed': the [clear light]{prabhasvara} absorbed in the body, which through the juice of ignorance has been put ante, 'outside'. The kāpālika is one who protects (pāl-) ka, conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, having set the vajra of mind in place (cp.18.m3).

In Shastri's text Munidatta's question is addressed to the 'purified avadhūtikā' (pariśuddhāvadhūtikā, with a folio number inside the word), although his introduction to the refrain names the unpurified one (apariśuddhāvadhūtikā); the Tibetan has 'unpurified' (yongs su ma dag pa'i) in both places, which suggests a lost a-. For upagamayati, 'turns to, brings near', the Tibetan has khro bar byed pa, 'makes angry'. The Tibetan of this segment breaks off at ka pA la ni (cp.18.m3).

tam̐ilo is tam̐i, 'you' (as agent), with lo, a vocative particle used to a woman. biṭaliu, 'spoiled', is a past form; later Bengali biṭāl- means ritual pollution by contact, the defilement an untouchable's touch was held to cause, and that may be the image here. The Tibetan line has rnam par nyams byed, 'ruin, cause to decay'; Munidatta's paraphrase uses ṭālita, the verb of 3b, explained as 'destroyed' (nāśitam), and has tayā, 'by her', where the song has 'you' (cp.18.m4).

kājaṇa kāraṇa is obscure. I take kājaṇa as a genitive plural of kāja, 'deed, work' (Sanskrit kārya), and kāraṇa as 'cause', together qualifying the moon. The Tibetan line, bya ba byed pa ri bong 'dzin pa 'joms, 'destroys the hare-holder that does the deed' (or 'deed, doer and hare-holder'), and Munidatta's 'the moon ... which has become the cause of clear light' (prabhāsvarahetubhūtam) both find a cause here (cp.18.m4). Other analyses: kāraṇa as 'for the sake of' ('for the sake of deeds'), or kāja ṇa kāraṇa, 'without deed or cause', 'for nothing'. ṭāliu is 'shaken from its place, toppled'; Munidatta explains it as 'destroyed' (vinaṣṭīkṛtam), and the Tibetan has 'joms, 'destroy, overcome'.

sasahara (Sanskrit śaśadhara, 'hare-bearer') is a common name for the moon, after the hare Indians see on its face; the Tibetan ri bong 'dzin pa, 'hare-holder', keeps the image. Toppling the moon is an impossible feat, in keeping with the sweep of 'you have spoiled everything'.

Munidatta says that with this couplet Kāṇha, going into detail, speaks against Ḍombī further (tām evoparāgayati; the verb is unusual). By her, the unpurified avadhūtī, the whole threefold world of gods, asuras, humans and the rest has been destroyed through [false knowledge]{mithyajnana}; and the [moon]{moon} (śaśahara) is conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, the cause of [clear light]{prabhasvara}, destroyed by 'the yoginī of those without the lineage' (asampradāyayoginī). He adds a line from 'the Caryā masters': [camphor]{camphor} fallen into a ditch is lost (cp.18.m4). The Tibetan comment has 'the yogin lacking instruction' (man ngag dang bral ba'i rnal 'byor pa) where the Sanskrit has the yoginī, and names the source of the camphor line glu dbyangs zhabs, 'the master of song'.

biruā is the adjective 'bad, ugly' (Sanskrit virūpa): biruā bolai, 'speaks ill'. The Tibetan has ngan par brjod, 'speaks badly'. The same spelling is the poet Virūpa's name in song 3, which is why the glossary matched it here.

Munidatta says this couplet states Ḍombī's true nature. Those who, ignorant of the true nature, do not know her as the purity of [innate joy]{sahajananda} speak against her, because under the power of karma they experience the suffering of saṃsāra. Certain [lords of yogis]{yogindra} (prādeśikāḥ, perhaps 'here and there'), who know her through the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the union of vajra and lotus, do not abandon her, day and night, at the throat, the [wheel of enjoyment]{sambhoga-cakra} (cp.18.m5). He then quotes a scriptural verse on 'some yogins, somewhere', who throb with joy in the meeting of [kakkola]{kakkola} with 'dear [bola]{bola}' and delight always in dwelling in the abode of the dead; he does not explain it.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rigs ldan skye bo khyod kyi mgul nas 'khyud, 'people of good family embrace you by the neck': 'of good family' where the Bengali has bidujaṇa, 'the wise', as if reading a word like kulīna, and a positive 'embrace' for 'do not let go'. The Tibetan of Munidatta's comment has 'gul ba, apparently for mgul ba, 'neck' (cp.18.m5).

melaī, 'lets go' (mel-, 'loosen, release'), with na, 'does not let go'; Munidatta's paraphrase has na parityajanti, 'do not abandon' (cp.18.m5). bidujaṇa loa, 'wise people', is rendered 'the wise'. torem̐ kaṇṭha is 'your neck'; holding her by the neck is presumably an embrace, as the Tibetan takes it.

Caṇḍālī: a woman of the Caṇḍāla community, whom caste society ranked lowest of all; kāmacaṇḍālī is 'the Caṇḍālī of desire' (kāma). 'Has sung the Caṇḍālī' keeps the construction in which she is what the song celebrates; the Tibetan line makes it 'the song of the Caṇḍālī of desire' ('dod pa gtum mo'i glu). Tibetan gtum mo also names the inner-fire practice of tantric yoga; that is a reading, not the sense of the line. gāitu is probably past (the Tibetan has blangs, 'sang'); Munidatta's paraphrase is present, gīyate, 'is sung' (cp.18.m6).

Munidatta calls the last couplet the praise of the yoginī. 'Such a Caṇḍālī', which he calls 'the means of practice for one who abides in action' (karmasthasādhanopāya, an obscure compound standing where the song has kāma), is sung by Kṛṣṇācārya alone and by no one else. Apart from Ḍombī there is no other 'woman with her nose cut off' (chinnanāsikā, the punishment of an unchaste woman) or 'woman of the town' (nāgarikā), since she establishes a ground of difference (bhedādhiṣṭhāna) according to the differences between beings; the sentence is obscure. He closes with a verse of the [Jñānasaṃbodhi]{tx-jnanasambodhi}: mind alone is the great seed of existence and [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}; in the conventional it becomes the conventional, in nirvāṇa, lack of intrinsic nature (cp.18.m6).

taāgali, 'beyond', can mean 'more than, surpassing' or 'apart from'. The Tibetan line, gdol pa mo las lhag pa'i dmangs rigs med, 'there is no low-caste woman surpassing the Caṇḍāla woman', takes it as surpassing, and has gdol pa mo, 'Caṇḍāla woman', for Ḍombī and dmangs rigs, 'low caste', for chiṇālī. Munidatta's ḍombīvyatirekāt, 'apart from Ḍombī', takes it as exclusion (cp.18.m6). 'Beyond' keeps both.

termsOmitted.reason: False match: biruā here is the adjective 'bad, ill' (Sanskrit virūpa) in biruā bolai, 'speaks ill' (the Tibetan has ngan par brjod, Munidatta viruddhaṃ vadanti), not the poet Virūpa, whose name the manuscript spells Biruā in song 3.

proposals.definition: Play or sport (Sanskrit līlā, Old Bengali līṛa): effortless, spontaneous activity, a favourite word of the siddhas for how the realized act. In song 18 Kāṇha falls asleep in the play of great bliss; Munidatta renders the word krīḍā, 'play', and says he went into yogic sleep in play (cp.18.m2). The Tibetan has rol, 'revel, play'.
proposals.rationale: Recurs in the songs and in Munidatta (for example līlayā, 'playfully', of going by the path of the avadhūtī); a fixed rendering keeps 'play' apart from 'ease' (helā) and from the game of dice (dyūta). The Tibetan match is limited to rol rtsed, since bare rol also occurs in pha rol, 'far side'.

proposals.definition: False or mistaken knowledge (mithyājñāna): cognition that takes things for what they are not, close to confusion (bhrānti) and ignorance. Munidatta says that Ḍombī, the unpurified avadhūtī, has destroyed the whole threefold world of gods, asuras and humans through false knowledge (cp.18.m4). The Tibetan has log pa'i shes pa.
proposals.rationale: A doctrinal term in Munidatta's comment on couplet 3 of song 18; an entry keeps it distinct from ignorance (avidyā), delusion (moha) and confusion (bhrānti) when the commentary is woven.

questions: Heading: I added the poet from the attribution kṛṣṇavajrapādānām printed before the song (removed from 1a by emendation), as 'Rāga Gauḍā · Kāṇha'. Do you want the poet in the heading at all, and if so as 'Kāṇha' (glossary form) or 'Kṛṣṇavajrapāda' (the attribution's wording, like 'Lūyīpāda' in the model heading)?

1a bāhia: I wrote 'I have rowed through the three worlds with ease', using the songs' usual sense of bāh- (and the reading the glossary's three-worlds entry already assumes). The song has no other boat; would you prefer something without the boat, such as 'passed through' or 'cast off' (nearer Munidatta's 'overcome'), or the Tibetan's 'enter'?

2a bhābhariālī is kept in source form as the glossary directs. Munidatta's 'by false imputation' points to something like pretence or show, the Tibetan's skra yags to 'fine hair'. Keep it untranslated, or choose an English word?

2b: I kept the refrain verbless: 'At the edge, high-born people; in the middle, the kāpālika.' Is 'at the edge' right for ante, or do you prefer 'outside' (Munidatta's bāhye)? Note that the Tibetan puts the kāpālika 'among' people of the edge lineage instead.

3a biṭaliu: I chose 'spoiled' to hold both 'defiled' (ritual pollution, later Bengali biṭāl-) and 'ruined' (Tibetan, Munidatta). Would you rather commit to 'defiled', which makes the caste image explicit?

3b kājaṇa kāraṇa: I followed both witnesses in reading a cause attached to the moon ('the moon, the cause of deeds'). Is that acceptable, or would you prefer 'for no reason' (kāja ṇa kāraṇa) or 'for the sake of deeds'? 'toppled' for ṭāliu: acceptable, or 'destroyed' with the witnesses?
5a: 'Kāṇha has sung the Caṇḍālī of desire' treats her as what the song celebrates (both witnesses agree). Is 'has sung' acceptable, or do you prefer 'sings of'?
Glossary: the p-virupa entry matched the adjective biruā ('bad') in 4a. Could its Old Bengali match be narrowed (for example to the bhaṇitā of song 3) so that it stops firing on this common word?
Commentary (for the weave): Shastri's Sanskrit in cp.18.m3 addresses the 'purified avadhūtikā' where the introduction and the Tibetan have 'unpurified'. Should the weave read apariśuddha there?
